title: Compassion in Action
subtitle: Four steps — and the two where people stop.
objectives: Name the four steps of compassion
Explain why the helper's identity matters

cards.title: Feeling sorry is not helping
cards.text: Compassion has four steps and almost everyone stops after two. The parable in Luke 10 is built to make that stopping impossible to miss.

cards.title: Notice, feel, move, cost
points: **Notice** — you actually see the person.
**Feel** — something moves in you.
**Move** — you cross the road.
**Cost** — it takes your time, money or plan.

cards.title: Six buttons
cards.text: Tap each step. The last two buttons are the point of the parable.

question.explain: Feeling sorry is where it usually ends.

cards.title: What the Samaritan actually did
cards.text: The detail in the text is specific, and the specificity is the point.
points: **He went to him.** That verb comes first.
**Oil, wine and bandages** — he used what he was carrying.
**He put him on his own animal** and walked.
**Two days' wages to the innkeeper**, and a promise to return.

question.text: What did the Samaritan leave with the innkeeper?
options: Two days' wages and a promise to return
question.explain: The cost was real and ongoing.

cards.eyebrow: The part that is easy to miss
cards.title: Who the helper was
cards.text: The audience's reaction to the word "Samaritan" is half the parable.
points: **A priest passed. A Levite passed.**
**Both were respected religious figures.**
**The one who stopped** was from a group the audience despised.
**That choice is deliberate.** Compassion is not about belonging.

cards.title: The glove touch after a knockdown
cards.text: Something real happens in boxing that is exactly this.
points: **A fighter who drops his opponent** often helps him up.
**Corners check on the other corner** after a bad stoppage.
**Nothing in the rules requires it.**
**It costs them nothing to skip** and they do it anyway.

cards.title: Reviving a teammate costs you
cards.text: The games that do this well make helping genuinely expensive.
points: **You stop, you are exposed, you lose time.**
**That is why it means something.**
**Help that costs nothing** is not really help.
**Step four is the cost.** The parable knew that.

question.text: Which step do most people stop at?

cards.title: Step three, in one picture
cards.alt: One hand gripping the forearm of another reaching up from below, taut with effort
cards.text: Noticing and feeling do not look like anything. This does.

cards.title: Bayanihan is step three and four
cards.text: After a typhoon the pattern repeats across the country.
points: **Neighbours clear a neighbour's roof** before their own.
**Relief packed by people** who were also hit.
**Nobody waits to be asked.**
**That is noticing, moving and paying** in one week.

cards.title: What to remember
points: Notice, feel, move, cost — four steps, not one feeling.
People stop between feeling and moving.
The Samaritan used what he carried, then paid and promised to return.
The helper was the one the audience least expected.

quiz.text: The four steps of compassion are…
quiz.objective: Name the four steps of compassion

quiz.text: Who passed by before the Samaritan?
What did the Samaritan put the man on?
What did he use on the wounds?
How much did he leave at the inn?
Why does it matter that the helper was a Samaritan?
options: He was from a group the audience despised
quiz.objective: Explain why the helper's identity matters

quiz.text: Matthew 9:36 says that seeing the crowds, he…
quiz.objective: Name the four steps of compassion

quiz.text: The priest and the Levite definitely felt nothing.
quiz.explain: They may well have felt it. They still walked past.

quiz.text: Help that costs the helper nothing is…
quiz.explain: The cost is what makes it compassion rather than sympathy.
quiz.objective: Name the four steps of compassion

quiz.text: Bayanihan after a typhoon shows which steps most clearly?
quiz.explain: People who were hit themselves pack relief for others.
quiz.objective: Name the four steps of compassion

quiz.text: The verb the parable turns on is…
quiz.explain: Crossing the road is the moment it becomes compassion.

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 3 Devotion. Compassion is broken into four verbs so that the gap between feeling and acting becomes visible and nameable. The Samaritan is read with its actual detail — what he carried, what he paid, what he promised — because the parable's force is in the specificity, and because a vague retelling lets the listener off. The week makes two points that are often skipped: the priest and Levite may well have felt something and still walked past, and the helper was from a group the audience despised, which is a deliberate choice in the text. The gaming lens gives the sharpest version of step four: help that costs nothing is not help.
discussion: Ask what the Samaritan actually paid and promised.
Ask why the storyteller chose a Samaritan.
extension: Have him do one thing this week that costs him time he wanted.
Have him retell the parable from the innkeeper's side.
misconceptions: "Compassion is a feeling." It has two more steps after the feeling.
"The priest did not care." The text does not say that; it says he passed.
"The Samaritan was a respected figure." He was the opposite.
